title: Lithium industry needs the equivalent of 134 new mines by 2050
gist: Benchmark forecasts lithium demand of about 7 million tonnes LCE in 2050, up 4.8 million tonnes from 2.11 million in 2026, equal to 134 new mines (average 36,000 t LCE) and more than US$100 billion of investment before recycling. The upside case implies about 180 mines and over US$150 billion, with recycling as the main swing factor.

insights.claim: The lithium industry needs the equivalent of 134 new mines by 2050 to meet demand, of which 44 are needed for demand growth between 2040 and 2050 alone.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale of supply build-out needed and its back-loaded component.

insights.claim: Benchmark forecasts global lithium demand reaching about 7 million tonnes LCE in 2050, 4.8 million tonnes above the 2.11 million tonnes in 2026, with 76% driven by EVs.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Demand more than triples, anchoring long-run lithium volume expectations.
insights.locator: Benchmark Mineral Intelligence forecasts that global lithium demand

insights.claim: At an average mine size of 36,000 tonnes LCE, the 4.8 million tonne demand increase equals a new mine roughly every two months for 24 years.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Illustrates the pace of project delivery required.
insights.quote: effectively a new mine every two months for the next 24 years
insights.locator: At an average mine size of 36,000 tonnes LCE

insights.claim: Meeting 2050 demand requires more than US$100 billion of investment before any contribution from recycling, according to Cameron Perks.
insights.speaker: Cameron Perks
insights.so_what: Sizes the capital needed for lithium supply.

insights.claim: Cameron Perks says the biggest challenge is sustaining lithium investment through price cycles while competing for capital with AI, defence and the wider energy transition.
insights.speaker: Cameron Perks
insights.so_what: Capital competition and price volatility, not geology, is the key constraint on lithium supply.
insights.quote: The biggest challenge is sustaining that investment through price cycles, while competing for capital with AI, defence and the wider energy transition.

insights.claim: Benchmark's capex analysis, which assumes recycling meets a significant share of demand, puts investment needed to meet 2040 lithium demand at around US$64 billion.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Gives a nearer-term investment benchmark that depends on recycling assumptions.

insights.claim: Batteries account for 92% of lithium demand in 2026, up from around 70% in 2020, and EVs account for 55% of demand, forecast to reach 76% by 2050.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Lithium demand is increasingly a battery and EV proposition.

insights.claim: Stationary storage lithium demand has grown more than 60% a year for two years but is expected to slow significantly to around 5% a year to the end of the decade.
insights.speaker: Cameron Perks
insights.so_what: Storage growth moderation reduces its contribution to near-term demand upside.
insights.quote: we expect that pace to slow significantly, to around 5% a year to the end of the decade

insights.claim: Australia is forecast to supply 29% of mined lithium in 2026 but only 20% by 2050 as mines deplete, financiers hesitate over price volatility and regulatory burden grows, even with expansions such as PLS's P2000 around 2030.
insights.speaker: Cameron Perks
insights.so_what: Australian share loss opens room for other regions unless local growth is backed.
insights.quote: Many of Australia’s mines will be depleting by 2050.
insights.locator: Australia is forecast to be the largest producer

insights.claim: China's share of mined lithium is forecast to stay stable around 25%, supported by domestic resource investment and battery supply chain dominance.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: China retains a stable supply anchor.

insights.claim: North American mined lithium supply is forecast to rise from 1.7% in 2026 to 13% by 2050, versus 6% of cell-production demand rising to 12%.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: North America moves toward domestic self-sufficiency, a policy-driven shift.
insights.locator: North American supply is set to increase

insights.claim: Europe supplies under 1% of mined lithium against 7% of cell-production demand today, and is forecast at 5.5% of supply versus 8% of demand by 2050.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team

insights.claim: Cameron Perks says large European and North American projects often need novel technology or face environmental and community concerns, causing delays and higher costs.
insights.speaker: Cameron Perks
insights.so_what: Western supply projects carry delay and cost risk.

insights.claim: In Benchmark's upside scenario of almost nine million tonnes LCE demand, the requirement rises to about 180 mines and well over US$150 billion.
insights.speaker: Cameron Perks
insights.so_what: Policy-driven demand upside could raise the investment need materially.
insights.locator: The number of mines could be significantly higher

insights.claim: Benchmark forecasts recycling will supply almost half of lithium by 2050, making it the biggest factor that could reduce new mines needed, but Cameron Perks says the base case asks a lot of it.
insights.speaker: Cameron Perks
insights.so_what: Recycling shortfalls would shift volume onto mines.
insights.quote: Every tonne that recycling doesn’t deliver has to come from a mine.

insights.claim: Recycling growth is limited by how quickly batteries reach end of life and by cost competition with mines.
insights.speaker: Cameron Perks
insights.so_what: Track end-of-life battery volumes and recycler cost curves.
